Inside the Growing Danger for Ethiopia's Humanitarian Workers 21 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — When humanitarian workers travel to the field, they carry more than food, medicine, or information. They carry the hopes of people facing hunger, displacement, illness, and conflict. Yet, the danger increasingly exposes those delivering this assistance. In Ethiopia, humanitarian workers have been killed, kidnapped, threatened, robbed, and caught in crossfire. Some have been abducted for ransom. Others have lost their lives while carrying out routine duties. These are not simply workplace accidents or unfortunate incidents. They raise serious questions about the protection of people who help others survive crises. The question is simple: Who protects the people who protect others? Ethiopia needs to move beyond telling aid workers to be careful. It needs a system that prevents avoidable harm, supports those affected, investigates serious incidents, and ensures that national and local responders are not left to carry the risks alone. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn From kidnappings to drone strikes Consider the death of Mahelet Sitotaw Abera, a staff member of ORDA Ethiopia. On 20 June 2025, she was collecting humanitarian data in Angot District, North Wollo, when she was critically wounded during crossfire between government forces and non-state armed groups. She died later that day. The United Nations condemned her death and called for the protection of humanitarian personnel. In 2024, Ethiopian NGO worker Yared Melese was abducted in North Wollo. His kidnappers demanded a ransom. His death was confirmed in August, according to The New Humanitarian's investigation . The danger is not limited to national organizations. On 24 June 2021, three Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) staff members --María Hernández Matas, Tedros Gebremariam Gebremichael, and Yohannes Halefom Reda--were killed in Tigray. In June 2026, MSF said the families had still not received the findings of a credible and impartial investigation. MSF's internal review had concluded that the clearly identified humanitarian workers were deliberately targeted. These incidents are different. Mahelet died during crossfire, Yared was abducted, and MSF maintains that its colleagues were deliberately targeted. They should not be treated as legally identical. But each raises urgent questions about prevention, protection, and accountability. No one should have to risk their life simply to help others survive." The wider situation remains concerning. On 30 September 2026, the UN Resident and Humanitarian Coordinator in Ethiopia reported that at least ten humanitarian vehicles had been seized by armed groups between 2025 and 2026, with only two recovered at the time of the statement. The UN also expressed concern about incidents affecting aid personnel, humanitarian assets, and premises. The global picture is equally troubling. According to the Aid Worker Security Database , 713 major incidents affecting aid workers were recorded in 2025, compared with 637 in 2024. A Reuters report published in August 2026 said that 907 aid workers were killed, injured, or kidnapped in 2025. These figures measure different aspects of violence and should not be confused: one counts recorded incidents, while the other counts people affected. On World Humanitarian Day, 19 August 2026 , the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) warned that armed drones were changing the risks faced by humanitarian workers. OCHA reported that 350 aid workers were killed, 322 injured, and 235 kidnapped worldwide in 2025. It also reported that, during the first part of 2026, a further 82 aid workers had been killed, 97 injured, and 39 kidnapped. The message was clear: public condemnation alone is not enough. States and parties to armed conflict must respect international humanitarian law and ensure accountability for violations. This threat has also become a direct concern in Ethiopia. On 20 September 2026, a humanitarian truck carrying approximately 41 tonnes of food assistance for internally displaced people in Sheraro, northwestern Tigray, was reportedly hit during drone strikes while travelling along a road in the region. Addis Standard reported the incident. The truck was transporting food intended for displaced families who depend on humanitarian assistance. Reports differed on the driver's injuries and how much of the cargo was lost, so those details should be treated cautiously. The attack drew international concern. Human Rights Watch reported that the United States condemned the strike on the humanitarian convoy. The incident is a serious warning: when humanitarian transport is hit, the danger extends beyond the driver and the vehicle. Food supplies may be lost, deliveries delayed, and already vulnerable families left waiting for assistance. The available reports establish that the convoy was struck, but responsibility for the attack should not be asserted without reliable evidence. The use of armed drones raises difficult questions for humanitarian protection. A vehicle carrying relief supplies may be exposed to attack even when it is travelling to support civilians. Humanitarian organizations must continually reassess security risks, protect staff and drivers, review routes and movement procedures, and ensure that personnel can stop a journey when conditions become unacceptable. But these measures cannot replace the responsibility of parties to a conflict to respect humanitarian personnel and relief operations under applicable international law. Behind every statistic is a person, a family, and a community that may lose access to essential assistance. Ethiopia needs credible investigations into serious incidents, public accountability where appropriate, and practical measures to prevent attacks from happening again. My Own Experience: Danger does not end when an incident is over My concern about aid-worker safety comes not only from reports and statistics but also from what I personally experienced while travelling through a conflict-affected area. On one occasion, armed men wearing military-style uniforms stopped several vehicles along the road. At first, we assumed they were government security personnel conducting a routine checkpoint inspection. We soon realized they were members of a non-state armed group impersonating security personnel. They ordered all passengers to get off the vehicles and lie face-down in muddy water beside the road. We were forced to remain there, unable to raise our heads, fearing for our lives. When a woman and two male passengers objected to the order, one of the armed men shot them. All three died in front of us. The armed men then took passengers' mobile phones, money, jewelry, watches, and other valuables. Several vehicles, including other buses, were looted. When we were finally released, I discovered that I had lost my laptop, camera, tablet, clothing, and other belongings. More painfully, I lost months of humanitarian assessment data, photographs, field documentation, and research materials. Their loss disrupted my work and meant that valuable information gathered in the field could no longer be used without significant effort to recover or reconstruct it. The effects went beyond material loss. I had witnessed three people being killed and feared for my own life. The experience reminded me that surviving a security incident does not mean its consequences end when the immediate danger passes. I share this experience because incident reports cannot fully capture the human cost of insecurity. Behind the statistics are people whose lives, families, work, and sense of safety are changed forever. When aid workers are attacked or robbed, humanitarian operations and the communities depending on them can also suffer. This must lead to action. Governments and parties to armed conflict must respect humanitarian personnel and their work. Humanitarian organizations and donors must provide realistic resources for staff protection, emergency support, and care for survivors and families. Serious incidents must be investigated, and those responsible must be held accountable where the evidence supports it. Protecting aid workers is not simply about protecting organizations or projects. It is about preserving the lifeline between people in crisis and the assistance they need. No one should have to risk their life simply to help others survive. Why do aid workers remain at risk? There is no single explanation. In conflict areas, humanitarian workers may be caught in fighting, deliberately attacked, kidnapped for ransom, or threatened because their work is misunderstood or politicized. Vehicles, supplies, and equipment may also be seized. Elsewhere, risks may arise from crime, extortion, administrative restrictions, community disputes, misinformation, or pressure from powerful local actors. The danger is not only about the threats workers face. It is also about how organizations prepare for them. Three factors help explain why the same environment can be more dangerous for some workers than for others. First, "threat" refers to the possibility of harm, such as armed violence, kidnapping, or detention. Second, exposure concerns how often and in what circumstances workers encounter that threat. Third, vulnerability describes the factors that make harm more likely or make it harder to prevent and respond to an incident. These are common elements of humanitarian security risk management. The Global Interagency Security Forum's Security to Go toolkit explains how aid organizations can assess risks and strengthen their security arrangements. For example, two organizations may operate in the same district, but one may have reliable communications, updated security information, and emergency medical arrangements, while the other lacks these resources. Their workers may face similar threats but have very different levels of protection. Research and humanitarian security guidance also point to an important responsibility: organizations must consider the risks faced by different groups of workers, including national staff. The Global Interagency Security Forum's guidance on managing the security of aid workers with diverse profiles highlights the relationship between a worker's circumstances, their role, and their organization's responsibility to take reasonable steps to protect them. A staff member may understand the risks and still feel unable to refuse a journey because a deadline is approaching, funding is limited, or a manager expects the activity to proceed. This is why security cannot depend only on an individual worker's judgment or courage. A credible protection system must allow workers to raise concerns, delay travel, and stop an activity when the risks become unacceptable. Managers must take these concerns seriously, and workers must not be unfairly penalized for refusing an unsafe assignment. This responsibility is also reflected in United Nations Security Council Resolution 2730 (2024) , which calls on states and parties to armed conflict to respect and protect humanitarian personnel and comply with applicable international humanitarian law. Protecting aid workers requires both respect for these legal obligations and practical action by humanitarian organizations to reduce foreseeable risks. Localization Without Resources: Shifting risk, not power National and local organizations are often close to the communities they serve. Their staff speak local languages, understand social relationships, and can reach people whom others may struggle to reach. Their knowledge is an important humanitarian asset. But local knowledge does not make local responders invulnerable. Localization must not mean that local people carry the risk alone." National staffs continue living in conflict-affected areas when international colleagues relocate. Local NGOs are expected to maintain assistance in dangerous locations while decisions about budgets, program deadlines and security arrangements are made elsewhere. Community volunteers, local health workers and informal responders face even greater challenges. They can be the first to respond to an emergency, yet have limited security training, insurance, emergency assistance or formal recognition. This does not mean that all international organizations provide adequate protection or that every national NGO lacks it. The issue is whether protection reflects the risks people actually face, rather than their job title, nationality or employer. Global funding evidence makes this concern difficult to ignore. A May 2026 study by ODI found that just below 10% of international humanitarian funding reached local and national actors directly and indirectly in 2024. Only 3.8% reached them directly. The report also found that local actors often receive shorter, smaller, and more restricted grants than international counterparts. These are global figures, not Ethiopia-specific estimates, but they illustrate the wider financing problem. When local organizations have limited funding for insurance, security management, emergency medical care and staff support, they struggle to protect the people expected to deliver assistance. This is the localization paradox: local actors are encouraged to lead, but the money, authority and protection needed to lead safely may remain elsewhere. As I argued in my earlier Addis Standard article , transferring responsibility to local organizations is not enough if resources and decision-making power do not follow. Localization must not mean transferring risk to local organizations while keeping control and protection resources elsewhere. Public Trust, Community Acceptance: Important, but insufficient substitutes for protection Humanitarian security often relies on three approaches: acceptance, protection, and deterrence. The Global Interagency Security Forum (GISF) identifies these as complementary elements of humanitarian security risk management. Acceptance means building trust with communities and relevant local actors. Organizations explain who they are, why they are present, how assistance is selected, and how people can raise complaints. They listen to concerns and correct mistakes. Protection involves practical measures such as risk assessments, safe travel arrangements, reliable communications, staff training, and emergency plans. Deterrence aims to discourage attacks through appropriate engagement, legal consequences, and action by responsible authorities. These approaches must work together. Community trust cannot replace practical safety measures, and neither can replace accountability. As GISF's guidance on community acceptance explains, acceptance requires sustained relationship-building and cannot be taken for granted. In Ethiopia, elders, religious leaders, women's groups, youth representatives, customary institutions, and local volunteers may help identify tensions, correct misinformation, and resolve disputes before they escalate. When people believe assistance is being distributed unfairly, for example, clear eligibility criteria and accessible complaints processes can help address concerns before they threaten staff safety. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) highlights the value of listening to communities, sharing information, and creating opportunities for feedback. Customary institutions, including the Gadaa system among Oromo communities , also offer lessons in mediation and collective responsibility. Their role must be understood in its specific context. Such institutions can contribute to trust, but they cannot guarantee safety or replace formal legal protection. Acceptance is not equal for everyone. Shared language, religion, ethnicity, or local identity may help some workers build relationships, while others may face suspicion or discrimination. Women may also experience gender-based harassment and other risks linked to how they are perceived. Two workers performing the same task may therefore experience different levels of safety. Organizations must recognize these differences without stereotyping communities or expecting local leaders to put themselves at risk to protect aid workers. Public perceptions also matter. People may question why some households receive assistance while others do not. Rumors, political accusations, and online misinformation can deepen suspicion and, in some circumstances, contribute to threats against humanitarian personnel. Humanitarian Outcomes' Aid Worker Security Report 2025 examines the changing security environment for aid workers, including concerns about declining acceptance and hostile narratives. The ICRC's guidance on harmful information explains how false or misleading information can undermine trust and put humanitarian workers and affected communities at risk. Humanitarian organizations must respond through transparency, accountability, and effective communication. They should explain assistance criteria, listen to complaints, and address legitimate criticism rather than dismiss it. Community radio, local-language discussions, schools, religious leaders, and trusted digital communicators can help explain humanitarian principles and why attacks on aid workers disrupt essential services. Trusted local content producers could help deliver accurate, accessible messages to wider audiences. However, campaigns must avoid political propaganda, protect sensitive information, and ensure that sharing stories or images does not expose staff or communities to further danger. The aim is to encourage informed public discussion, not to silence criticism or portray every critical voice as hostile. Awareness must also reach relevant government institutions, military personnel, and armed actors. Under applicable international humanitarian law, humanitarian relief personnel are entitled to protection in the circumstances set out in the relevant rules. Article 71 of Additional Protocol I to the Geneva Conventions addresses personnel participating in relief actions, while Rule 31 of the ICRC's Customary IHL Study sets out the customary rule on the protection of humanitarian relief personnel. Public awareness alone is not enough. Training, engagement with authorities and military command structures, credible investigations, and accountability for violations must reinforce these legal obligations. Ultimately, communities can help create a safer environment, and responsible communication can strengthen trust. But humanitarian workers must not be left to depend on goodwill alone. Community acceptance is one part of protection; the responsibility to respect applicable law, protect humanitarian personnel, and hold perpetrators accountable remains essential. From legal promise to practical reality International humanitarian law provides important protection for humanitarian relief personnel during armed conflict, subject to the applicable legal rules. The International Committee of the Red Cross identifies the protection of humanitarian relief personnel in customary international humanitarian law. In May 2024, the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2730, calling on states and parties to armed conflict to respect and protect humanitarian personnel and to address impunity for violations. These protections are not favors. They reflect legal obligations. However, having laws is not the same as enforcing them. Serious incidents must be documented and investigated through appropriate channels. ethiopia.title: Obituary - Prominent Kenyan Oromo Scholar, Anthropologist Professor Abdullahi Shongolo Passes Away
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Obituary - Prominent Kenyan Oromo Scholar, Anthropologist Professor Abdullahi Shongolo Passes Away - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Obituary - Prominent Kenyan Oromo Scholar, Anthropologist Professor Abdullahi Shongolo Passes Away 21 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Professor Abdullahi Shongolo, a prominent scholar of history and anthropology whose research on Borana Oromo culture, customary law, and history brought international attention to the community's rich heritage, passed away on 20 October at the age of 68 at Nanyuki Hospital in Kenya, following an illness from which he did not recover. Born in 1958 in Moyale, Kenya, Professor Shongolo completed his education in Kenya. He worked in various parts of the country and served in Kenya's Ministry of Education, rising to the position of Assistant Director of Education. Jaatani Diidaa, a cultural and historical researcher, told Addis Standard that Professor Shongolo devoted much of his life to in-depth research, making significant personal sacrifices to bring the educational and cultural heritage of the Oromo of Kenya and Ethiopia to international attention. Professor Shongolo made substantial contributions to anthropological research, serving as a senior researcher at Germany's renowned Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology for more than two decades, from 1999 to 2019, according to Jaatani. During the 2000s, he also served as an Associate Research Fellow in the Department of Social Anthropology at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden, where he pursued research and academic work. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn Among his major scholarly contributions were books co-authored with prominent German scholar Professor Günther Schlee, including Pastoralism and Politics in Northern Kenya and Southern Ethiopia and Islam and Ethnicity in Northern Kenya and Southern Ethiopia . He also documented traditional Borana oral literature and proverbs in Boran Proverbs in Their Cultural Context . These works helped bring greater international recognition to Oromo history, pastoral life, religious traditions, and customary systems of governance, particularly the Oromo customary governance, Gumii Gaayo Assembly. Professor Shongolo's passing "has brought profound grief and shock to the Borana Oromo community, the wider Oromo community across the world, and people in Kenya and Ethiopia, as well as to scholars in the international academic community, Jaatani said. ethiopia.title: Entrenched Authoritarianism: Ethiopia's Rule of Law Index Slides Further
ethiopia.content: Ethiopia: Entrenched Authoritarianism: Ethiopia's Rule of Law Index Slides Further - allAfrica.com AllAfrica English (current) En Français Toggle navigation My Account Toggle navigation AllAfrica My Account English (current) En Français Ethiopia: Entrenched Authoritarianism: Ethiopia's Rule of Law Index Slides Further 21 October 2026 Addis Standard (Addis Ababa) Addis Abeba — Ethiopia's rule of law performance has deteriorated further, with the country ranking 133rd out of 143 countries and jurisdictions in the 2026 World Justice Project (WJP) Rule of Law Index, according to the ranking provided for this report. The latest assessment extends a multi-year decline that has seen the country remain near the bottom of global and sub-Saharan African comparisons. The 2026 index, released on 21 October, comes as the WJP warns that authoritarian practices are becoming entrenched worldwide, with weakened checks on executive power, declining judicial independence and restrictions on fundamental freedoms contributing to a prolonged global deterioration in the rule of law. The WJP said the global rule-of-law recession had continued for a ninth consecutive year, with 62% of the countries and jurisdictions assessed recording declines, compared with 38% that improved. Although the share of countries experiencing deterioration fell from 68% in 2025, the overall direction remained negative. The latest findings reinforce concerns about institutional accountability and civic freedoms in Ethiopia, where successive editions of the index have documented persistent weaknesses in constraints on government authority, fundamental rights, open government and the enforcement of regulations. Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn A sustained decline across successive editions Ethiopia's latest ranking follows a pattern documented by Addis Standard in previous years. In the 2025 edition, the country ranked 132nd out of 143 countries, with its overall score falling by 2.4% from the previous year to 0.36. It placed 30th among 34 countries in sub-Saharan Africa, highlighting the depth of its institutional weaknesses relative to regional peers. The decline has persisted across multiple editions. Ethiopia ranked 129th out of 142 countries in 2023, with a score of 0.38, after placing 123rd out of 140 countries in 2022. In the 2024 edition, it ranked 130th out of 142 countries, recording a further 2.4% fall in its overall score. The successive declines point to a longer-term deterioration rather than a one-year fluctuation. They also come against a backdrop of armed conflicts, restrictions on civic freedoms and concerns over the independence and effectiveness of public institutions. Checks on government power, fundamental rights remain weak The 2025 index offers a detailed picture of the areas contributing to Ethiopia's poor performance. The country ranked 134th globally for constraints on government powers, 138th for fundamental rights, 135th for open government and 137th for regulatory enforcement. Its rankings were somewhat higher in civil justice, at 124th, and criminal justice, at 104th. It ranked 96th for absence of corruption. The figures suggest that the weakest areas extend beyond the operation of courts. They include the mechanisms through which government decisions are scrutinized, public institutions are held accountable and citizens exercise fundamental freedoms. The WJP's constraints-on-government-powers measure assesses whether those exercising public authority are bound by law and subject to institutional and non-governmental checks. These include legislative oversight, judicial limits on executive authority and the role of an independent press in holding government to account. Ethiopia's low ranking in this category is particularly significant given longstanding concerns about the relationship between political authority and independent institutions. The country's scores in open government and fundamental rights also point to persistent challenges involving access to information, civic participation and freedoms of expression, assembly and association. The index does not, by itself, establish the cause of every institutional weakness or determine responsibility for individual violations. It provides a comparative assessment based on surveys of households and legal practitioners and experts, capturing how the rule of law is experienced and perceived. Authoritarian practices have become entrenched In its 2026 global findings, the WJP identified the expansion of authoritarian practices, the narrowing of civic space and the weakening of checks and balances as the principal forces behind the continuing global decline. "Authoritarianism is no longer merely an emerging trend - it has become entrenched in many parts of the world," Alejandro Ponce, the WJP's executive director, said in the report's accompanying statement. The organization said more than 86% of countries and jurisdictions had experienced sustained five-year declines in at least one of three safeguards against authoritarian rule: constraints on government powers, open government or fundamental rights. The latest assessment also found that freedom of opinion and expression declined in 64% of countries, freedom of assembly and association in 67%, and civic participation in 65%. Judicial limits on government power deteriorated in 63% of countries, while civil justice weakened in 64% and criminal justice in 58%. The WJP said undue executive pressure and government interference were major drivers of institutional deterioration in both civil and criminal justice systems. Although these are global findings rather than Ethiopia-specific figures, they provide context for the challenges reflected in Ethiopia's repeated low rankings. The country's performance in constraints on government power, fundamental rights and open government places those concerns at the center of its rule-of-law record. Conflicts and restrictions on civic space form part of the wider context Ethiopia's ranking comes amid continuing insecurity and serious human rights concerns across several regions. Armed conflicts in Amhara, Oromia and parts of Tigray have contributed to a difficult environment for civilian protection, access to justice and the exercise of basic freedoms. Addis Standard has previously reported on extrajudicial killings, torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearances, as well as restrictions on freedom of expression and assembly. A U.S. State Department assessment of Ethiopia's 2024 human rights record, reported by Addis Standard in August 2025, documented abuses attributed to state and non-state actors in the context of ongoing conflicts. The media environment has also remained under pressure. In March 2026, Addis Standard reported on an assessment by International Media Support documenting continued intimidation, detention and harassment of journalists in Ethiopia. The report recorded at least 44 journalists abducted or detained during 2025, compared with 43 in 2024. Such developments are relevant to the rule-of-law assessment because the index considers not only whether laws exist, but also how effectively institutions protect rights, enforce legal safeguards and constrain the exercise of public power. However, the index's aggregate score does not independently establish a direct causal relationship between any single conflict, detention or restriction and Ethiopia's overall ranking. Rather, its indicators provide a broader framework for assessing institutional performance alongside other documented evidence. Regional position underscores Ethiopia's decline Ethiopia's 2025 position of 30th among 34 sub-Saharan African countries placed it near the bottom of the regional table. Its overall score of 0.36 was substantially below those of regional leaders, including Rwanda, Namibia and Mauritius. The regional picture is itself mixed. The WJP has reported broad deterioration across sub-Saharan Africa, although some countries have recorded improvements in particular years. Ethiopia's continued low placement nevertheless points to the difficulty of reversing the institutional weaknesses identified in successive editions. Globally, the 2026 index covers 143 countries and jurisdictions and draws on more than 215,000 household surveys and 3,400 surveys of legal practitioners and experts. It assesses eight dimensions: constraints on government powers, absence of corruption, open government, fundamental rights, order and security, regulatory enforcement, civil justice and criminal justice. Scores range from zero to one, with higher scores indicating stronger adherence to the rule of law. The annual index is designed to measure how people experience the rule of law in practice, rather than simply whether a country has laws, courts or formal constitutional protections with its findings offering a comparative view of the relationship between legal institutions, public accountability and everyday access to justice. The victory sends Somalia into Monday’s final against Uganda, which had already secured its place in the championship match. Somalia, the 2022 CECAFA U-17 champions, will be seeking another regional title. advertisements After a goalless first half, Rwanda took the lead when substitute Patrick Ujeneza dribbled past two Somali defenders before beating goalkeeper Khalid Nor. Somalia responded four minutes later through Mohamud Osman, who scored after Rwanda’s defenders failed to clear the ball. With the score level at 1-1 at the end of regulation time, the match went to a penalty shootout, where Somalia prevailed 5-4. “I am so happy that my players remained focused and came from behind to score and later win in penalties,” Somalia coach Dadir Ami Ali said. “We now go and prepare for the final against a strong Uganda team.” The result continues Somalia’s campaign in the regional qualifying tournament for the 2027 TotalEnergies CAF U-17 Africa Cup of Nations. Somalia’s Minister of Youth and Sports, Mohamed Abdukadir Ali, and Somali Football Federation President Ali Abdi Mohamed Shiine, who also serves as vice president of CECAFA, congratulated the players and coaching staff following the victory. The officials praised the team's performance and determination in reaching the final. Somalia previously won the CECAFA U-17 Championship in 2022 and will have an opportunity to claim another title when it faces Uganda on Oct. 19. Meanwhile, Rwanda will face Ethiopia in a third-place playoff on the same day, with the winner securing the region’s third qualifying berth for the 2027 CAF U-17 Africa Cup of Nations. Somali President Mohamed Abdullahi Mohamed also declared drought, which has been ravaging the Horn of Africa nation, a national disaster last month. (Xinhua/Sun Ruibo/IANS) Mogadishu, Oct 22 (IANS) Imminent flooding could displace nearly 874,000 people in Somalia over the next three months, the International Organisation for Migration (IOM) warned Thursday. Heavy rainfall and rising rivers now threaten communities already struggling with drought and repeated displacement, the UN migration agency said in a statement, urging international support for preparedness and early action. "There is still time to reduce the impact, but that window is closing. We urgently need funding to help people protect their homes and livelihoods, reach safer ground where necessary, and avoid another cycle of displacement," said Manuel Marques Pereira, chief of mission for IOM in Somalia. New projections by IOM and the Danish Refugee Council estimate that 874,319 people could be displaced between October and December, with flooding driving 92 per cent of that displacement, Xinhua News Agency reported. The warning comes as Somalia enters its rainy season, which is forecast to bring above-normal rainfall driven by strengthening El Nino conditions. According to IOM, signs of flooding are already emerging across the country. The Jubba River at Dollow is approaching flood levels, while the Shabelle River at Jowhar is rising toward the top of its banks. Heavy rainfall in Baidoa has already damaged homes, forcing families to flee several neighbourhoods. Despite the mounting crisis, IOM said it has secured just 14.4 per cent of the 16.62 million dollars needed to respond to the impending El Nino floods. The severe funding shortfall jeopardises critical relief efforts aimed at supporting over 517,000 vulnerable people across flood-prone areas of Somalia, it said. IOM said rising floodwaters threaten to wipe out crops, devastate livelihoods, contaminate water supplies, and cut off access to healthcare and essential services, further deepening crisis levels in communities already battered by successive climate shocks. According to IOM, while it is working with Somali authorities and local partners to strengthen early warning systems, map evacuation routes, and prepare emergency aid, acute funding shortages are bottlenecking critical response efforts. "Without immediate resources, plans to build safe relocation sites and deliver emergency shelter, clean water, sanitation, and healthcare remain severely constrained," IOM said. IOM called for urgent international support to scale up early action before rising floodwaters displace hundreds of thousands more families. enrolls citizens returning from Yemen for biometric national IDs National ID enrollment aims to help returning citizens access public services as Somalia expands its digital government infrastructure Oct 22, 2026, 1:40 pm EDT | Ayang Macdonald Categories Biometrics News | Government Services | ID for All Somalia’s National Identification and Registration Authority (NIRA) has begun issuing biometric national ID cards to citizens returning from Yemen to support their reintegration and access to public services. NIRA made the announcement on October 21, stating that the exercise was carried out in collaboration with the National Commission for Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons (NCRI). The returnees are being hosted at a reception camp managed by the commission. According to the ID authority, its Deputy Director General, Abdirahman Said Ahmed, visited the center recently where the returnees were being enrolled for biometric ID, and assured them that NIRA would facilitate access to identity services needed for their social and economic reintegration. Somalia launched its biometric national ID system in 2023. NIRA says approximately two million people have been enrolled, with citizens encouraged to use the eAqoonsi mobile application for services. There is a target to reach 15 million enrollments by 2029, an objective supported by ongoing efforts by NIRA to get the national ID integrated with many public services including banking, passports, and domestic travel. Extending the biometric national ID to the Yemen returnees is part of Somalia’s identity inclusion efforts as authorities believe obtaining a national ID will help them engage with the service delivery infrastructure that the government is building for the wider population. That infrastructure includes the planned launch of a unified digital government service platform, Halmeel, bringing together government services through a one-stop platform. Details about this plan were discussed this week in an interview with Biometric Update, when Halmeel’s Director General, Mohamed Dubo, said they expect to bring together approximately 70 government services through a common interface. He said the platform will cover services including passport and national ID issuance, business registration, driver’s licenses, vehicle documentation and education certificates. Expected to be launched by the end of March 2027, the unified digital government platform will allow users to submit requests, track applications, and make payments for these public services. Somalia’s initiative reflects broader efforts to use national identity systems to improve access to services for displaced populations, including Ethiopia’s Fayda programme and Namibia’s issuance of biometric ID cards to refugees. This point was emphasized at the ID4Africa Annual General Meeting in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire, in May, where Dr. Patrick Eba, Deputy Director at the UNHCR’s International Protection and Solutions Division, called for the building of more inclusive identity systems that enable refugees and stateless persons to access essential services in their host countries. somalia.summary: Somalia's National Identification and Registration Authority (NIRA) has initiated a program to enroll citizens returning from Yemen into its biometric national ID system. This effort, announced on October 21, aims to facilitate the reintegration of these returnees into society and improve their access to public services. The enrollment process is conducted in collaboration with the National Commission for Refugees and Internally Displaced Persons (NCRI), which manages a reception camp for the returnees. NIRA's Deputy Director General, Abdirahman Said Ahmed, assured the returnees of support in accessing identity services essential for their social and economic reintegration. Since launching its biometric ID system in 2023, Somalia has enrolled around two million individuals, with a goal of reaching 15 million by 2029. This initiative is part of a broader strategy to integrate the national ID with various public services, including banking and travel, and is aligned with global efforts to enhance identity systems for displaced populations.

Former Prime Minister Mohamed Hussein Roble was among the opposition figures who congratulated Liban and welcomed his election, in a move that has drawn criticism over the opposition’s consistency on electoral matters. The development comes amid escalating tensions between the opposition and the federal government, with the two sides at odds over the country’s electoral process. Opposition leaders have previously denounced similar elections held in Banadir region and South West State by the Mogadishu-based administration of President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud through the same electoral body. Their decision to welcome the Galmudug election has therefore raised questions about the apparent discrepancy between their previous objections and their current position. Analysts have described the move as a political own goal, arguing that it could undermine the opposition’s credibility and weaken its efforts to challenge President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s push for an electoral process that could secure his re-election. The perceived inconsistency could present a significant challenge for opposition leaders as they seek to build a coherent position against the president’s electoral agenda. The meeting focused on enhancing collaboration in military training, developing the knowledge and skills of SNA personnel, and elevating the standards of training programmes to build a professional, prepared national force capable of responding to the country’s security obligations. Both sides emphasized the importance of continued cooperation and support to improve the quality, capacity, and capability of the Somali National Army. A New Commander for a Longstanding Mission General Falasca’s appointment marks the latest leadership transition for EUTM-Somalia, which has operated since 2010 and remains one of the EU’s most enduring military engagements in Africa. He succeeded Brigadier General Elio Manes, who had led the mission since January 2026, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the EUTM leadership transition . During his tenure, General Manes oversaw training programmes for SNA officers and maintained regular engagement with Somali military leadership, including a May 2026 meeting with General Mahmoud to discuss capacity building and sustainable security, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of EUTM’s engagement with Somali forces . The mission has also supported advanced training for senior SNA officers at the Dhagabadan Military School, with Manes personally attending graduation ceremonies. General Falasca inherits a mission that has trained thousands of Somali soldiers over nearly two decades, but whose role is evolving as Somalia prepares to assume full responsibility for its own security. The EU has approved €75 million for the AU mission in Somalia, and EU-funded initiatives such as the SNA III Project under the European Peace Facility are designed to professionalize the Somali National Armed Forces through structured training, operational planning support, and logistical capacity-building, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the security transition . Italy’s Dual Role in Somali Training General Falasca’s command of EUTM-Somalia coincides with Italy’s deepening bilateral defense engagement with Mogadishu. In October 2026, the Commander of the SNA’s Training and Doctrine Command, Major General Ahmed Isse Ahmed, visited Italy’s Training and Doctrine Command headquarters in Turin and the Italian Special Forces School to discuss expanding Italy’s support for Somali military training. Italy is the largest contributor to EUTM-Somalia and also leads the Bilateral Training Mission for Somali and Djiboutian Police Forces (MIADIT Somalia) through the Carabinieri. This dual-track approach, combining EU mission leadership with bilateral training initiatives, gives Rome a uniquely comprehensive role in Somalia’s security sector reform. The SNA has also pursued training partnerships beyond Europe. General Mahmoud has presided over Danab Special Forces graduation ceremonies at the Balidoogle military base, where U.S.-supported training resumed in June 2026 after a suspension following a ration-diversion scandal, as reported in FTL Somalia’s coverage of the Danab training programme . The elite unit has been described by AFRICOM commanders as one of the most capable forces on the continent. Critical Note The meeting between General Mahmoud and General Falasca is a routine engagement between a host nation’s military leadership and the commander of a training mission that has operated in the country for over a decade. It signals continuity in the EU-Somalia security partnership at a moment when that partnership faces significant questions about its endgame. EUTM-Somalia has trained thousands of Somali soldiers. It has supported the development of military institutions, from the Dhagabadan Military School to the Training and Doctrine Command that General Ahmed heads. These are tangible contributions. But the mission’s ultimate purpose, to build a Somali army capable of securing the country without external support, remains unfulfilled. The SNA continues to depend on international partners for training, equipment, logistics, and pay. EUTM’s mandate has been extended repeatedly, not because Somalia is ready for independence, but because the conditions for a full handover have not yet been met. The appointment of a new commander is an opportunity to reassess. General Falasca inherits a mission that is well-intentioned and well-resourced, but whose impact on the SNA’s operational effectiveness is difficult to measure. Training is necessary. It is not sufficient. The gap between the number of soldiers trained and the number of soldiers who remain in service, properly equipped and led, is the gap that determines whether EUTM’s work produces a lasting force or a revolving door. The new commander’s tenure will be judged by whether that gap narrows. somalia.content: Netanyahu’s Somalia Map Revives Fears of Partition عربي English Türkçe اردو فارسى Friday, 23 October 2026 - 12 Jumada Al-Ula 1448 AH Gulf Arab World World Opinion Interviews Varieties Business Culture Sports Entertainment Fashion Features Technology Gulf Arab World World Opinion Interviews Varieties Business Culture Sports Entertainment Fashion Features Technology عربي English Türkçe اردو فارسى Skip to main content Latest News Netanyahu’s Somalia Map Revives Fears of Partition Port Security and Trade Continuity: A New Formula for Saudi Competitiveness Iraq Fears Return of ‘Shadow Factions’ to Regional ‘Unity of Fronts’ Campaign Netanyahu’s Somalia Map Revives Fears of Partition https://english.aawsat.com/world/5332475-netanyahu%E2%80%99s-somalia-map-revives-fears-partition World Netanyahu’s Somalia Map Revives Fears of Partition From the Somali capital, Mogadishu (Reuters) Cairo: Mohamed Mahmoud 18:30-22 October 2026 AD ـ 11 Jumada Al-Ula 1448 AH T T Cairo: Mohamed Mahmoud 18:30-22 October 2026 AD ـ 11 Jumada Al-Ula 1448 AH T T Netanyahu’s Somalia Map Revives Fears of Partition From the Somali capital, Mogadishu (Reuters) A map unveiled by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has sparked outrage in Somalia, which accused him of undermining its sovereignty and territorial integrity by depicting Puntland and Somaliland as separate states. The map has reignited fears of partition in a country already grappling with deep divisions. Puntland remains at odds with the federal government, while Israel recognized the breakaway region of Somaliland several months ago. Somalia rejects the map Somalia's federal government "categorically rejected" what it called a "misleading map" displayed during Netanyahu's news conference on Sunday, saying it portrayed the country as fragmented. It condemned the move as "a flagrant violation of Somalia's sovereignty, territorial integrity and internationally recognized borders." In a statement issued by the Information Ministry on Wednesday evening, the government reaffirmed its unwavering commitment to national sovereignty and the unity of its territory and people. It stressed that Somaliland and Puntland remain "integral and inseparable parts of the unified, sovereign Somali state." The government warned that any attempt by foreign officials or outside parties to redraw Somalia's political map, misrepresent its borders or undermine its territorial unity would constitute a direct violation of international law and diplomatic norms. It urged the international community and its partners to respect Somalia's independence and territorial integrity, pledging to uphold its constitutional duty to defend the country's sovereignty and national unity. Netanyahu displayed the map, titled "Geopolitical Alliances in the Middle East," during an Israeli national security briefing on Oct. 18. It placed Puntland and Somaliland in geopolitical categories linked to Israel. For Mogadishu, the controversy goes beyond the map itself. Abdulwali Jama Barre, an African affairs expert and co-founder of the Somali Academy of Leadership and Global Affairs, said the government's response underscored its determination to preserve Somalia's unity and reject any treatment of its regions as independent states. But Barre drew a distinction between the map's depiction and formal recognition of independence. "Showing Somali territories under separate geopolitical classifications does not, in itself, mean the map formally declared them independent states," he told Asharq Al-Awsat. "However, the Somali government viewed the depiction as fragmenting the country's political map and undermining its internationally recognized borders." Barre said the dispute carried particular weight given Somaliland's contested political status, its ties with Israel and fears in Mogadishu that foreign involvement could weaken Somalia's unity. The deeper concern, he said, is that foreign powers could increasingly treat Somali regions as entities separate from the federal state. That risk would grow if symbolic gestures were followed by concrete steps or new formal arrangements amid the country's existing political disputes, he added. Deep divisions Somaliland's strategic location adds another dimension to the dispute. The breakaway region stretches along 740 kilometers of the Gulf of Aden coastline, occupying a key position at the junction of the Indian Ocean and the Red Sea in the Horn of Africa. It is also home to the strategically important Port of Berbera. Since breaking away from Somalia in 1991, Somaliland had failed to secure international recognition until Israel recognized it, a decision Mogadishu firmly rejects, with Arab countries backing its position. The map controversy comes as tensions between Somalia's federal government and Puntland remain unresolved. In May, Puntland President Said Abdullahi Deni declared that he no longer recognized Hassan Sheikh Mohamud as Somalia's legitimate president, accusing him of illegally abusing his presidential powers. Deni called for an urgent gathering of Somalia's political parties to agree on an inclusive electoral process. The dispute is part of a broader rift between Puntland and Mogadishu. Over the past year, the regional administration has repeatedly challenged Mohamud's positions and refused dialogue with him. Deni has also joined the opposition Somali Future Council, which is demanding the government's departure. At the time, Somalia's federal Interior Minister Ali Yusuf Ali, known as Hosh, sharply criticized Deni, calling him "an obstacle to the state, the country's unity and its development." Barre warned that such internal divisions must be addressed through constitutional and political dialogue to prevent disputes between Mogadishu and regional administrations, particularly Puntland, from becoming an arena for foreign competition. He urged Mogadishu to pursue diplomatic action on several fronts, beginning with a formal protest to Israel and a request for clarification about the map and the circumstances in which it was presented. Somalia should also raise the matter with the United Nations, African Union, Arab League and Organization of Islamic Cooperation, seeking assurances of respect for its sovereignty and territorial integrity, he said. At home, Barre stressed the need for renewed dialogue between the federal government and regional administrations, especially Puntland, to resolve their differences within an agreed constitutional framework. He urged Mogadishu to pursue diplomatic action on several fronts, beginning with a formal protest to Israel and a request for clarification about the map and the circumstances in which it was presented. Somalia should also raise the matter with the United Nations, African Union, Arab League and Organization of Islamic Cooperation, seeking assurances of respect for its sovereignty and territorial integrity, he said. At home, Barre stressed the need for renewed dialogue between the federal government and regional administrations, especially Puntland, to resolve their differences within an agreed constitutional framework. المجموعات، الذي من المقرر أن ينطلق في أواخر شهر نوفمبر . ومن أبرز مفاجآت الجولة ما حدث في مدينة مصراتة، حيث فاز "السويحلي" الليبي على "الترجي" التونسي بنتيجة 1-0، مما يضع العملاق التونسي أمام ضرورة تقديم أداء قوي في مباراة الإياب على أرضه لتجنب الخروج المبكر من البطولة . كما يواجه حامل اللقب "ماميلودي صنداونز" مباراة إياب مصيرية، بعد تعادله سلبياً (0-0) أمام "ويليتي" الأنغولي في مدينة لوبانغو . وفي المقابل، حقق "رينجرز إنترناشيونال" النيجيري واحدة من أبرز نتائج جولة الذهاب بفوزه على "مولودية الجزائر" بنتيجة 2-0 في مدينة أبيوكوتا . كما تصدر "سكوتلاند إف سي" الزيمبابوي المشهد بفوزه على أرضه بنتيجة 2-0 على "بترو أتلتيكو" الأنغولي، بفضل هدفين سجلهما اللاعبان الدوليان السابقان "خاما بيليات" و"نوليدج موسونا"، ليمنحا فريقهما انتصاراً ثميناً. وحقق فريق "يانغ أفريكانز" التنزاني أكبر فوز خارج أرضه في هذه الجولة، بتغلبه على "سي إف إف إيه " (CFFA) من مدغشقر بنتيجة 4-0، كما استهل فريق "نهضة بركان" المغربي مشواره بنجاح بفوزه خارج دياره على "ستار سبورت أكاديمي" من سيراليون بنتيجة 2-0 . وعاد فريق "الهلال" السوداني من إثيوبيا بفوز ثمين بنتيجة 2-0 على حساب "بن سيداما "، بينما تألق فريق "كولومب سبورتيف" الكاميروني خارج ملعبه أيضاً، محققاً الفوز على "تينغيث" السنغالي بنتيجة 2-0 في داكار . وتسعى هذه الأندية الأربعة الآن للحفاظ على تفوقها وضمان التأهل إلى دور المجموعات . كما حقق كل من "الزمالك" و"بيراميدز" المصريين الفوز خارج أرضهما بنتيجة 1-0، مما عزز فرصهما في التأهل، في حين انتزع "أورلاندو بايرتس" الجنوب أفريقي فوزاً ثميناً خارج ملعبه على "أفريكان ستارز" الناميبي بنتيجة 1-0 . وتأمل هذه الأندية الثلاثة في استغلال ميزة اللعب على أرضها في مباريات الإياب الحاسمة . من جانبه، يواجه فريق "تي ​​بي مازيمبي" -الفائز باللقب الأفريقي خمس مرات- رحلة صعبة إلى تونس، بعد تعادله بنتيجة 1-1 على أرضه في لوبومباشي أمام "النادي الأفريقي" التونسي . كما حقق "أسيك ميموزا" الإيفواري تعادلاً ثميناً بنتيجة 1-1 خارج ملعبه أمام "المغرب الفاسي". وفي مواجهة أخرى اتسمت بالندية، تغلب "إف سي سان بيدرو" الإيفواري على "إف سي نواذيبو" الموريتاني بنتيجة 2-1، مما يجعل حظوظ الفريقين قائمة في مباراة الإياب بموريتانيا . أما فريق "هورويا" الغيني، فسيسافر لمواجهة "المريخ" السوداني وهو يحمل في جعبته تقدماً ضئيلاً بنتيجة 1-0، بعد فوزه في كوناكري . ونظراً لأن فارق هدف واحد فقط يفصل بين الفريقين، فإن مباراة الإياب تعد بمواجهة أخرى قوية ومحتدمة . وضعت النتائج المسجلة في مختلف أنحاء القارة عدداً من الأندية العريقة أمام خطر الإقصاء المبكر، في حين باتت فرق أخرى طموحة على أعتاب التأهل إلى دور المجموعات. مع اقتراب مباريات الإياب الحاسمة، تستعد المنافسة لعطلة نهاية أسبوع أخرى مليئة بالمواجهات الحاسمة حيث تسعى الأندية المتبقية إلى حجز مكان لها في دور الـ16 في أفريقيا . دوري أبطال أفريقيا توتال انرجيز التصريحات تشتعل.. الهلال يرد بعنف ويهاجم رئيس اتحاد الكرة السوداني الهلال السوداني السودان كرة قدم حافظ محمد أحمد الخرطوم winwin أضفنا الى 'غوغل' أثارت تصريحات معتصم جعفر سر الختم، رئيس الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم، خلال مؤتمره الصحفي الأخير، ردود فعل غاضبة بعد أن حمّل نادي الهلال السوداني مسؤولية خسارة المنتخب الوطني أمام نظيره الموزمبيقي في تصفيات كأس أمم أفريقيا . واستنكرت إدارة الفريق الأزرق تبرير رئيس الاتحاد، الذي أرجع الهزيمة إلى تأخر انضمام لاعبي الفريق إلى معسكر "صقور الجديان"، نتيجة ارتباطهم بمباراة ودية أمام أهلي طرابلس الليبي، مما أربك ترتيبات سفرهم. إدارة الهلال السوداني تستنكر تصريحات سر الختم من جانبه، وصف رامي كمال، عضو مجلس إدارة الهلال السوداني تصريحات رئيس الاتحاد بأنها "جانبت الصواب" وتعد محاولة للهروب من المسؤولية، وشدد كمال على رفض النادي إقحامه في نتائج المنتخب، مؤكدًا أنّ الهلال ظل داعمًا للاتحاد السوداني انطلاقًا من مسؤوليته الوطنية وحرصه على مصلحة الكرة السودانية. كما دعا كمال إلى ضرورة تقييم نتائج المنتخب بناءً على أسس فنية وإدارية موضوعية، بعيدًا عن تحميل الأطراف الأخرى المسؤولية، أو إطلاق تصريحات قد تضر باستقرار المنظومة الكروية في البلاد. اقرأ أيضًا الهلال السوداني يصنع الحدث و"غربال" على موعد مع المجد اتحاد الكرة يحسم مستقبل مدرب منتخب السودان كواسي أبياه وأكد إداري الهلال السوداني إدراك الجميع للظروف الاستثنائية التي تعمل في ظلها منظومة كرة القدم السودانية، مشيرًا إلى أن ناديه جزء أصيل من هذه المنظومة، وأن مجلس إدارته يعمل بجد مع شركائه، وفي مقدمتهم الاتحاد السوداني لكرة القدم وبقية الأندية، لتجاوز التحديات الراهنة وضمان استمرارية النشاط الرياضي وتطويره. كما شدد على أنّ المرحلة الحالية تتطلب من جميع الأطراف التحلي بروح المسؤولية المشتركة، وتعزيز الحوار والتنسيق، والمشاركة الفاعلة في اتخاذ القرارات الاستراتيجية التي تخدم الكرة السودانية وتدفع بمسيرتها نحو الاستقرار، بدلًا من تبادل الاتهامات عبر وسائل الإعلام. واختتم بالتأكيد على أنّ رفضهم لتصريح رئيس الاتحاد لا يعني إنكار الجهود الإيجابية التي يبذلها الدكتور معتصم جعفر وأعضاء مجلس إدارته في دعم الأندية المشاركة في البطولات الأفريقية باسم السودان، مؤكدًا على أنّ اختلاف الرأي لا يلغي أهمية العمل المشترك لمصلحة الكرة السودانية، كما عبّر كمال عن ثقته بقدرة منتخب السودان على تجاوز كبوة مباراة موزمبيق، وتحقيق نتائج إيجابية في الاستحقاقات القادمة تضمن تأهله إلى بطولة أمم أفريقيا. النشرة البريدية اشترك معنا بالنشرة البريدية لتصلك آخر أخبار الرياضة اشترك معنا دول كرة القدم الأخبار الدوريات الفرق رياضات التنس كرة السلة رياضات ميكانيكية مبارايات اليوم الأخبار football.summary: الهلال السوداني رد على تصريحات رئيس اتحاد الكرة السوداني، الذي انتقد أداء الفريق في الدوري. جاء الرد من إدارة الهلال عبر بيان رسمي، حيث أكدت أن الانتقادات غير مبررة وأن الفريق يسعى لتحقيق النجاح رغم التحديات. كما أشار الهلال إلى التزامه بتطوير كرة القدم في السودان ودعم اللاعبين. البيان شدد على أهمية التعاون بين الأندية والاتحاد لتحقيق الأهداف المشتركة، ودعا إلى التركيز على تحسين الأداء بدلاً من الانشغال بالتصريحات. هذه الحرب الكلامية تعكس التوترات الحالية في الساحة الرياضية السودانية، حيث يسعى كل طرف لتأكيد موقفه.
